tagline: Cape houses, cranberry bogs and marsh views along the old highway
intro: Old King's Highway is a 34-mile National Scenic Byway through a Cape Cod landscape of marsh views, cranberry bogs and stretches framed by trees. The Federal Highway Administration highlights its combination of scenery and historic buildings: the drive passes through eight National Register districts, with early Cape houses, sea captains' homes and Victorian buildings along the way.

In Barnstable, this was the principal east-west road, linking the town's main population centers from the late 1630s. As maritime business shifted toward the southern villages in the early 19th century, construction along the old highway declined. That slowdown left a concentration of Federal and Greek Revival buildings. Barnstable Village remained the county’s civic center as its economic importance declined. The Route 6A number came later: it first appeared between Bourne and Barnstable in 1953 as the Mid-Cape Highway opened, then extended toward Orleans in 1956.

Traveling east, the road leads from Bourne through Sandwich to Barnstable, then Yarmouth and Dennis before reaching Brewster and Orleans. In Brewster, Route 6A becomes Main Street through the town center; Drummer Boy Park holds the Old Higgins Farm Windmill beside the route. At Orleans, Routes 6A and 28 join before ending at the Route 6 rotary on the Eastham town line.
notice: Trees frame sections of the road, with cranberry bogs and bayside marsh views along the corridor.

moments.title: Sandwich
moments.text: Sandwich's glass industry left a neighborhood as well as glassware. Deming Jarves founded the Boston & Sandwich Glass Factory in 1825; its lead glass became known for its color. Jarves also patented improvements to glass molds and pressing techniques. In Jarvesville, most of the historic district's contributing properties are homes built between 1825 and 1860, when the company was at its height. Modest Cape and Greek Revival houses sheltered glassworkers. The industrial buildings were eventually demolished in the 20th century. The houses continued to be occupied, including by glassworkers' descendants and workers from other industries.

moments.title: Old King's Highway Historic District, Barnstable
moments.text: The old county courthouse on Route 6A became a place of resistance on September 27, 1774. Protesters demanded that county officials refuse to obey the Massachusetts Government Act, which had stripped the colony of rights of self-government. The officials agreed, effectively ending royal control of the county. The building later changed purposes: in 1842 it was remodeled for the Third Barnstable Baptist Church. After that congregation disbanded in 1972, the nonprofit Tales of Cape Cod purchased it. This is one of two remaining Massachusetts colonial courthouses where the 1774 protests took place.

moments.title: Brewster
moments.text: Brewster's sea captains helped shape the town's architecture. Wealthy captains and commercial businessmen built Italianate, Greek Revival and Second Empire homes here during the 19th century. The town's surviving captains' houses include the Cobb House of 1799, now home to the Brewster Historical Society. There is another kind of working history at Drummer Boy Park on Route 6A: the Old Higgins Farm Windmill dates to 1795. The park also has a blacksmith shop and walking trails. Along the town's northern shore, the Brewster Flats spread out as tidal sand flats on Cape Cod Bay.
